vignette:
He is 37, a Latin American man who has spent most of his adult life working in social ministry, the kind of work that asks him to sit with other people’s suffering and make room for it. He says that before his marriage fell apart, he used to believe he was good at recognizing pain early, in others and in himself. Now he says this with a faint, embarrassed smile, as if he no longer fully trusts his own judgment.

He meets his former partner in his late twenties through church outreach. At first, he experiences her as passionate, devoted, and fiercely protective of him. He is drawn to her intensity. They work side by side on food drives and youth events, and he admires how quickly she can command a room. The first moments that trouble him seem small enough to explain away. She grabs his wrist hard during an argument in the car because she wants him to stop “walking away emotionally.” Later she cries, apologizes, and tells him he makes her feel abandoned. He wants to be compassionate. In his work, he often asks people to see the hurt beneath harmful behavior, and he does the same at home.

Over time, the violence becomes harder to minimize. During arguments, she shoves him against walls, throws objects, slaps him, once knees him hard in the thigh when he tries to leave the apartment. He learns to track the shifts in her mood with exhausting precision—the silence that stretches too long, the clipped tone, the way drawers close a little harder than usual. He becomes careful in his own home, measuring words, adjusting his posture, trying to keep his body loose and nonthreatening. What shames him most is not only the fear but the disbelief that follows it. He is a large man, physically capable, and he thinks, Who would believe this is happening? He worries that if he tells anyone, they will hear only that there was “mutual conflict,” or assume that because he works in ministry he should have handled it better.

The night that stays with him most vividly begins with something ordinary: dishes in the sink, both of them tired, a disagreement that should have ended in irritation and sleep. Instead, she accuses him of disrespecting her in front of friends. He tries to leave the kitchen to cool down. She blocks the doorway, then strikes him in the face with an open hand, again and again, before shoving him backward into the counter. He remembers the sharp edge digging into his lower back, the metallic smell of the faucet, the strange slowness of his thoughts. When he lifts his arms to shield himself, she throws a mug that shatters near his shoulder. He does not hit her back. He says what he remembers most clearly is the sound of his own voice pleading, low and careful, as if calming a frightened animal. Afterward, he locks himself in the bathroom and sits on the floor until morning, listening for footsteps.

Something changes in him after that. He still goes to work, still leads prayer circles, still visits families in crisis, but his body begins acting as if danger is always near. A slammed office door sends a jolt through his chest. If a couple raises their voices during a community meeting, his mind goes blank and his skin goes cold. At night he lies awake listening for movement in the hallway even after the divorce, sometimes checking the apartment lock three or four times before bed. When he does sleep, he wakes drenched in sweat from dreams in which he is trapped in kitchens, corners, narrow rooms with no exit.

He also begins avoiding parts of his own life. He turns down home visits if he is told a husband and wife are both present. He stays late at the ministry office because the quiet apartment feels too exposed. Friends invite him to gatherings, but he often declines, already tired from the effort of appearing calm all day. He is especially uncomfortable around conversations about intimate relationships. When colleagues speak casually about “red flags” or joke that men cannot really be afraid of women, he laughs with them a beat too late, then feels sick with anger at himself.

He talks about the divorce as if it is both finished and still happening. He knows he is physically safe now, yet he continues to scan parking lots, mirrors, and church entrances. Some part of him expects to see her, or someone like her, already watching. He is harder on himself than he is on anyone else. He calls himself weak for staying, weak for hiding it, weak for still reacting. But another part of him grieves the man he was before his home became a place of calculation and fear.

What stands out is how alone he has felt inside the experience. In ministry he is the steady one, the listener, the person others trust with their most painful stories. It unsettles him that when the story is his, words fail. Even now, while describing the worst nights, he watches my face closely, as if preparing for doubt. He speaks quietly, with long pauses, and sometimes apologizes for becoming emotional. Yet beneath the shame and vigilance, there is also a tired honesty. He says he wants, more than anything, to walk into his own apartment at night and feel that he has arrived somewhere, instead of bracing for what might happen next.
